the binnacle — a cell that holds the compass so the helmsman can see it in any light
the breakwater — a cell that is built to be hit, so the cells behind it are not
the clinometer — a cell that asks 'how far over am I?' and reports in degrees
the coaming — a cell that raises the edge of a hatch so water does not run down into the cabin
the companionway — a cell that is a stair from the deck to the cabin, and also a hatch you can close
the davit — a cell that holds the boat's small boats over the side, ready to lower
the dog — a cell that holds a hatch open against the motion of the sea, so the crew does not have to
the ebb — a cell whose value is the tide going out, and also the slack water that follows it
the ebbing — a cell whose value is the rate at which the water is leaving
the ensign — a cell that is a flag, and also a declaration of which nation the boat belongs to
the fairway — a cell whose value is the path through a channel that has been cleared
the fathom mark — a cell painted on the anchor chain every fathom, so the captain knows how much rode is out
the flood — a cell whose value is the tide coming in, and the strength of the current it brings
the galley stove — a cell that burns and cooks and heats the cabin and is the warmest place on a cold boat
the grounding — a cell whose value is the moment a boat touches bottom, and what is found there
the gudgeon — a cell that holds a pin that holds a rudder that turns a boat
the halyard — a cell that lifts a sail up the mast, and a person up the mast too if they have to go
the hatch cover — a cell that is also a door, and also a table, and also a bench
the hawse pipe — a cell through which the anchor chain leaves the hull
the inboard — a cell that is the part of the engine inside the hull, and the part of the crew that stays inside
the inhaul — a cell that pulls a sail into the boat, opposite of an outhaul
the island — a cell that other cells orbit but never reach
the jack — a cell that is a flag flown from the bow to show the boat is in harbor
the jackline — a cell that runs fore and aft on a boat, so a person can clip on and not fall off
the jackstay — a cell that runs the length of the deck so anyone can clip on
the kedge anchor — a cell that is a small anchor for a small boat, ready when the big one is not enough
the keel — a cell that runs the length of the hull and keeps the boat upright when the wind pushes
the knott — a cell whose value is one nautical mile per hour, and is measured by a chip log thrown over the side
the lanyard — a cell that is a short line attached to anything that might be dropped overboard
the lee board — a cell lowered on the downwind side to stop the boat from sliding sideways
the lee shore — a cell whose value is the shore you don't want to be downwind of
the limber hole — a cell that lets water drain to the bilge, so it can be pumped out
the main sheet — a cell that controls the main sail, and is the first thing a beginner learns to hold
the mast step — a cell that holds the mast in place and transmits the rigging's pull to the hull
the messenger — a cell that is a light line used to pull a heavy line through a block from far away
the nautical almanac — a cell whose value is the position of every star for every hour of every year
the navigator — a cell that is a person, and a person is a fabric of small decisions made while looking at a chart
the navigator's ruler — a cell used to measure distance on a chart at the latitude you actually are
the oarlock — a cell that holds the oar so the rower can pull without the oar sliding away
the oilskin — a cell that is a coat, and is also a metaphor for the boundary between the wet boat and the dry crew
the outhaul — a cell that pulls the foot of the sail out to the end of the boom, so the sail catches more wind
the painter — a cell that ties the dinghy to the mother ship with a single line
the peak — a cell that is the highest point of a gaff-rigged sail, and also the highest point a person can reach
the pinnacle — a rock that just below the surface looks like nothing, but from above is a mountain
the pinrail — a cell that holds the pins for the lines, so they are not lost and not tangled
the quarter — a cell that is the side of a boat between amidships and the stern, and also the wind that comes from there
the quay wall — a cell that is a wall, and also a place where a boat can lay alongside without anchoring
the quay — a cell that is also a wall, and also a place to tie a ship
the reef — a cell that is also a sail, and also a knot, and also a place where the boat would die if it hit one
the rode — a cell that is the line between the boat and the anchor, and what the wind is pushing against
the rosette — a cell whose shape is a flower made of knot-work, joining three lines in one
the rudder post — a cell that takes the captain's hand on the wheel and moves the water
the sea anchor — a cell that drags in the water to slow the boat when no sail is set
the shroud — a cell that is a standing rigging that holds the mast up sideways, against the wind
the sister — a cell that is a clip on a boat that holds two halyards together so they do not slap
the stanchion — a cell that holds a lifeline, so a falling crew member does not leave the boat
the stern light — a cell that shines only backward, so other boats know you are there
the telltale — a cell that is a thread tied to a sail so the sailor can see the wind the sail cannot feel
the thole pin — a cell that is the pivot for an oar when there is no oarlock
the tide gauge — a cell that records not the tide but the time the tide last turned
the topping lift — a cell that holds the boom up when the sail is not raised, so it does not fall on the crew
the uncleat — a cell whose value is the moment the line is released from the cleat and the sail fills
the uphaul — a cell that pulls a sail up, the opposite of a downhaul
the upwelling — a cell whose value is cold water rising from the deep to replace warm water blown away
the vang — a cell that pulls the boom down when the wind tries to lift it, so the sail does not twist
the variation — a cell whose value is the difference between true north and magnetic north, and which drifts
the wake — a cell that is created by the boat's passage and then read by the next boat
the warp — a cell that is a line moved from one boat to another to pull them together
the waterline — a cell that paints itself on the hull at the level the boat actually floats
the windward mark — a cell at the upwind edge of a racecourse, which every boat must round
the xebec — a small three-masted ship that could sail closer to the wind than any square-rigger
the yard — a horizontal spar hung from a mast, from which a square sail is bent
the yardarm — a cell from which things are hung high above the deck, in plain view of all
the yawl — a cell that is a small boat with two masts, the smaller one stepped abaft the rudder post
the zephyr — a cell that is a wind so light it can be told from a true calm only by the way it touches a cheek
the zinc — a cell that is a metal that corrodes instead of the propeller, and is replaced every year
